findings.headline: Network Optimisation project approved to proceed to procurement targeting £150,000 recurring annual efficiency, intended to fit within existing £781,000 budget with explicit contingency to bring revised financial case back if costs exceed envelope.
findings.detail: Proposal to redesign and refresh Council's network to simplify, improve resilience and reduce maintenance costs. The £150,000 recurring efficiency reflects expected reduced overhead and complexity. Proposal "is intended to be contained within the existing annual network budget of £781,000 wherever possible, subject to formal procurement and tender evaluation." However, explicit provision added: "If procurement confirms that additional one-off implementation costs or recurring cost pressures cannot be contained within the existing budget envelope, a revised financial case will be brought back for approval before contract award."
findings.matters: The contingency language indicates cost uncertainty on a material project; any budget pressure would add to the council's overall financial pressures and the £31M gap.
findings.figures: £150,000 full-year efficiency target, £781,000 existing annual budget
findings.quote: The proposal is intended to be contained within the existing annual network budget of £781,000 wherever possible, subject to formal procurement and tender evaluation. [...] If procurement confirms that additional one-off implementation costs or recurring cost pressures cannot be contained within the existing budget envelope, a revised financial case will be brought back for approval before contract award.

findings.headline: Council's £1.865M savings figures form monitoring baseline pending validation through delivery, procurement and benefits tracking
findings.detail: Paper identifies that "the savings profile is not delivered in full or within the required timescales" as the main financial risk, arising from workstream delays, scope changes, procurement outcomes, slower service redesign, workforce changes, supplier cost pressures or benefits realisation failure. Risks to be managed through clear savings ownership, finance validation, monitoring against baseline, procurement controls, benefits tracking and programme governance.
findings.matters: For a council with a £31M budget gap, tracking whether planned savings are delivered or deferred is critical to financial planning and identifying emerging pressures; explicit risks flag material uncertainty around delivery.
findings.figures: £1.865M savings target, baseline to be validated
findings.quote: These figures form the monitoring baseline and will be validated through delivery, procurement, workforce planning and benefits tracking.

findings.headline: Council's savings plan includes reduction of 31.4 full-time equivalent posts (6 per cent of Core Directorate workforce) to be achieved through vacancies, turnover and role redesign where possible.
findings.detail: Workforce impacts arise from service redesign, automation and technology simplification across customer experience, technology roadmap and process efficiency programmes. Council describes impact as "indicative at this stage" and subject to further validation through detailed design and implementation. Changes to staffing levels to be managed through established HR, consultation and governance processes, with redundancies mitigated where possible through natural workforce movements.
findings.matters: Workforce costs typically represent the largest element of council spending; planned reductions show where councils are finding productivity gains and signal whether savings targets are realistic or stretch.
findings.figures: 31.4 FTE reduction, 6% of Core Directorate workforce
findings.quote: The programme has employee implications because delivery of the Theme 2 Innovation and AI savings profile includes an indicative workforce impact of 31.4 full-time equivalent posts across the programme. [...] Wherever possible, employee implications will be managed through vacancies, turnover, natural wastage and the redesign of roles and responsibilities to mitigate the impact of potential redundancies.

findings.headline: Council requires £445,500 one-off investment in 2026/27 for Customer Contact as a Service platform replacement, with payback targeted by end of 2028/29 and planned full-year savings of £409,596.
findings.detail: Investment replaces outdated 8x8 contact centre platform with Microsoft Customer Contact as a Service. Business case identifies key risks including migration, integration, service continuity, adoption and benefits realisation. Savings delivery is conditional: "These savings are dependent on successful implementation, service redesign, channel shift, automation and delivery of the associated workforce efficiencies."
findings.matters: Shows specific capital commitment and expected return; the explicit dependency on benefits realisation and successful implementation flags execution risk that could affect whether this portion of the savings target is met.
findings.figures: £445,500 investment 2026/27, payback by end 2028/29, £409,596 full-year savings
findings.quote: The proposal requires one-off net investment of £445,500 in 2026/27, after allowing for the existing licensing budget and contribution from Microsoft. The business case shows payback by the end of 2028/29 and cumulative annual savings of £409,596 once the model is fully implemented. These savings are dependent on successful implementation, service redesign, channel shift, automation and delivery of the associated workforce efficiencies.

findings.headline: Council plans £1.865M savings from Theme 2 Innovation and AI plan over 2026-2029 MTFS period as part of response to £31M estimated budget gap.
findings.detail: Programme encompasses four connected areas: customer experience (reducing avoidable contact), technology roadmap (simplifying systems and licenses), process efficiency (process redesign and automation), and enabling development (culture change support). Delivery is phased, with minimal savings in 2026/27 (when £445,500 investment is made), £638,839 in 2027/28, and £1,137,715 in 2028/29, reaching full-year effect of £1,864,888.
findings.matters: The £31M budget gap is material; how councils plan to close it shows their approach to financial sustainability, and tracking whether this plan's £1.865M contribution is achieved will be central to understanding emerging financial pressures.
findings.figures: £31M budget gap, £1.865M from Theme 2, full-year effect £1,864,888
findings.quote: This report seeks Cabinet approval for the proposed Theme 2: Innovation and AI plan, which supports delivery of the 2026 to 2029 Medium Term Financial Strategy by contributing £1.865M towards the Council's savings requirement.

findings.headline: Efficiency contributions reduce MTFS gap by £0.639m (2027/28) and £1.138m (2028/29), but substantial shortfalls remain.
findings.detail: The plan's efficiency contributions reduce the MTFS gap from £11.678m to £11.039m in 2027/28 and from £23.286m to £22.148m in 2028/29. These savings address only a portion of the council's projected shortfalls, leaving significant funding gaps that require additional action.
findings.matters: Lenders and peer finance directors would need to assess whether these efficiency targets are realistic and whether the council has credible strategies to close the remaining gaps of £11m+ in 2027/28 and £22m+ in 2028/29.
findings.quote: Effect of this report 0.445 -0.639 -1.138 [...] Revised Medium Term Financial Strategy 0.445 11.039 22.148

findings.headline: Council invests £0.445m in customer experience from earmarked reserves in 2026/27 as part of innovation and AI plan.
findings.detail: The plan allocates £0.445m to Customer Experience Investment in 2026/27, financed from earmarked reserves. This is part of the Core Services Theme 2 MTFS Innovation and AI Plan. The investment is designed to generate efficiency contributions from 27-30 efficiency plans: £0.639m in 2027/28 and £1.138m in 2028/29.
findings.matters: Finance directors would need to track whether reserve drawdowns are sustainable and whether innovation/AI investments can realistically generate the claimed efficiency gains to help address the council's projected budget gaps.
findings.figures: Customer Experience Investment £0.445m (2026/27); Efficiency contributions £0.639m (2027/28), £1.138m (2028/29)
findings.quote: Customer Experience Investment 0.445 0.000 0.000 0.000 0.445 [...] To be Financed from: Earmarked Reserves 0.445 0.000 0.000 0.000 0.445

findings.headline: All four major implementation risks rated Amber; benefits realisation contingent on delivery of phased savings and 11 FTE efficiencies
findings.detail: The business case identifies four major risks all assessed as Amber: migration and service continuity; user adoption and benefits realisation; supplier delivery and cost control; and security and compliance. The financial case is explicitly sensitive to implementation costs, funding assumptions, dual-running duration and benefits timing.
findings.matters: All major risks rated Amber indicates active supervision is required. Lenders assess delivery risk to MTFS-dependent savings; delays or low adoption would reduce and delay benefits.
findings.figures: Four Amber-rated risks; phased savings dependent on delivery of 11 FTE efficiencies
findings.quote: The business case is most sensitive to assumptions on channel shift, automation, reduced avoidable contact, cost control and delivery of 11 FTE efficiencies. Delays, competing priorities or low adoption would reduce and delay the benefits.

findings.headline: Microsoft ECIF funding contribution of £84,500 subject to confirmation through procurement; if not secured, funding gap would widen
findings.detail: The business case assumes a potential Microsoft End Customer Investment Fund contribution of up to £84,500 to offset gross implementation costs of £500,000. This contribution is explicitly subject to confirmation through procurement and commercial discussions, meaning it is not yet secured.
findings.matters: Unconfirmed funding within a capital business case represents MTFS headroom risk. Lenders track assumed versus confirmed funding when assessing available resources.
findings.figures: ECIF contribution up to £84,500 (unconfirmed); gross implementation cost £500,000
findings.quote: Potential for Microsoft End Customer Investment Fund (ECIF) contribution up to £84,500 subject to confirmation through procurement and commercial discussions.

findings.headline: Dual-running with 8x8 platform until November 2027 identified as key affordability pressure; extension would delay payback and reduce cumulative annual saving
findings.detail: The business case flags running both 8x8 (£155,000 annual cost) and Microsoft CCaaS (£140,000 annual cost) in parallel until November 2027 as the key affordability pressure. If this overlap extends beyond the planned exit date, payback would be delayed and the cumulative annual saving available to the MTFS would reduce.
findings.matters: This is a known cost control risk with defined endpoint. Lenders track cost discipline; the council has identified this as the critical control point for affordability.
findings.figures: 8x8 annual cost £155,000; Microsoft CCaaS annual cost £140,000; planned overlap until November 2027
findings.quote: The key affordability pressure is dual running until 8x8 ends in November 2027.

findings.headline: Affordability of proposal explicitly conditional on three interdependent factors: approved funding package, controlled dual-running costs, and delivered savings profile
findings.detail: The council states the proposal is affordable only if the revised funding package including ECIF contribution is approved, dual-running costs are actively managed until November 2027, and the planned savings profile is delivered. This is a material statement of delivery dependency.
findings.matters: Explicit affordability conditions signal identified risks to MTFS sustainability. Lenders assess whether MTFS targets are based on realistic delivery assumptions.
findings.figures: Phased savings £69,756 and £115,572 in 2027/28; £209,268 in 2028/29; equivalent to 11 FTE efficiencies
findings.quote: This position remains affordable only if the revised funding package is approved, dual-running costs are actively managed and the planned savings profile is delivered.

findings.headline: £35,904 one-off MTFS funding requirement to cover gap between net implementation investment and captured cumulative savings
findings.detail: The net investment required is £445,500 but the cumulative annual saving once fully implemented is £409,596, leaving a one-off shortfall. This gap is explicitly flagged as needing to be contained within the MTFS.
findings.matters: This is an explicit call on MTFS headroom that lenders and peer councils track. The project is not wholly self-funding from within the payback period.
findings.figures: £445,500 net investment; £409,596 cumulative annual saving; £35,904 one-off gap
findings.quote: *The one-off gap of £35,904 (£445,500-£409,596) will be contained within the MTFS

findings.headline: Capital investment of £500,000 with payback achieved by end of 2028/29 and cumulative annual savings of £409,596 once fully implemented
findings.detail: The proposal requires a one-off implementation cost of £500,000 in 2026/27 with a managed transition period while exiting the current 8x8 platform. After dual-running and transition costs, the council moves into annual surpluses from 2027/28, achieving payback by end 2028/29 with cumulative annual savings of £409,596.
findings.matters: This is a material capital outlay with defined payback period and ongoing revenue benefit that directly supports MTFS objectives. Finance directors track capital deployment, payback periods and delivery risk.
findings.figures: £500,000 implementation cost; £445,500 net investment 2026/27; £96,995 surplus 2027/28; £224,268 surplus 2028/29; payback by end 2028/29; cumulative annual savings £409,596
findings.quote: The proposal requires a one-off implementation cost of £500,000 in 2026/27 and a managed transition period while the council exits 8x8. The Financial Case shows a year 1 deficit, followed by annual savings in 2027/28 and 2028/29. Payback is achieved by the end of 2028/29, with cumulative annual savings of £409,596 delivered once the model is fully implemented.

findings.headline: Implementation is scheduled for September 2027, meaning £150,000 workforce efficiency cannot be realized until late 2027 at earliest, with procurement and delivery risks that could delay benefits further.
findings.detail: The indicative timeline shows tender issue in December 2026, mobilisation in June 2027, and implementation in September 2027. Benefits tracking begins from go-live. The risks register identifies "Procurement delay" as an explicit risk that "Governance or procurement activity could delay delivery." Any slippage beyond this timeline extends the gap before benefits can be achieved.
findings.matters: Timing of savings realization is critical to MTFS planning. If the council has assumed this saving for 2027/28, slippage beyond September 2027 creates a financial gap and delays achievement of required efficiency targets.
findings.figures: Implementation scheduled Sept 27 (September 2027); tender Dec 26 (December 2026)
findings.quote: Implementation, migration and early life support Sept 27

findings.headline: The £671,000 annual network cost baseline underpinning the affordability case has not yet been validated.
findings.detail: The business case assumes existing network running costs of £671,000 for licences, connectivity, support and maintenance, but the financial case table identifies that this figure requires validation: "Finance and Technology to validate existing costs across licences, support, connectivity, maintenance and contracts." If the baseline is incorrect, the affordability assumption is invalid.
findings.matters: The entire cost-containment case depends on accuracy of the existing cost baseline. An incorrect or incomplete baseline makes the affordability test meaningless and suggests additional investment may actually be required.
findings.figures: £671,000 annual running costs (unvalidated)
findings.quote: Finance and Technology to validate existing costs across licences, support, connectivity, maintenance and contracts.

findings.headline: Network redesign is identified as a critical dependency for the Theme 2 Innovation and AI savings plan within the MTFS.
findings.detail: The paper states the project is essential for other planned productivity and savings initiatives: "A simplified, secure and cloud-optimised network is required to support automation, artificial intelligence adoption, digital service redesign and workforce productivity at scale. Without this network change, the Council will retain unnecessary complexity, continue to rely on ageing infrastructure and be less able to release the planned savings from the Innovation and AI theme."
findings.matters: Failure or significant slippage on this project cascades to other planned savings across the council. Lenders and peer finance directors need to understand if the MTFS has critical dependencies that could unravel if this technology project does not deliver.
findings.figures: No specific figures, but part of Theme 2 Innovation and AI savings plan
findings.quote: The project is a direct dependency for the Theme 2 Innovation and AI savings plan.

findings.headline: £150,000 annual workforce saving from 3 FTE reduction is dependent on successful project delivery, with delivery risk and timing risk affecting when benefits can be realized.
findings.detail: The proposal targets "an estimated efficiency of approximately £150,000 per annum" through headcount reduction, described as "a key financial benefit" and reduction in design-team effort. However, the risks register identifies that "Savings and operational benefits may be delayed or reduced," and benefits tracking begins only from September 2027 implementation onwards.
findings.matters: The council has likely incorporated this saving into MTFS planning. Delivery risk on the project directly threatens achievement of planned savings, potentially creating a gap in the financial plan if the project slips or delivers less efficiency than assumed.
findings.figures: £150,000 per annum; 3 FTE headcount reduction; £260,000 current network support and architecture team cost
findings.quote: A key financial benefit of the proposed operating model is a planned headcount reduction of 3 FTE, generating an estimated efficiency of approximately £150,000 per annum.

findings.headline: Project affordability within the existing budget remains contingent on procurement outcomes, with additional approval required if costs exceed the £781,000 envelope.
findings.detail: The financial case is based on an affordability assumption rather than a tested cost. Soft market testing "did not provide sufficiently complete or consistent financial information to confirm a final cost at this stage." The council states it does not currently make a confirmed additional investment request, but "If procurement identifies a one-off implementation cost or recurring cost pressure that cannot be contained within the existing budget, this will be returned for approval before contract award."
findings.matters: A major technology project is proceeding to procurement on an affordability assumption rather than tested costs, creating material risk that additional investment will be required and need separate approval.
findings.figures: £781,000 annual budget; £671,000 annual running costs; one-off implementation cost TBC; recurring managed service cost TBC
findings.quote: The financial case is currently based on an affordability assumption rather than a final priced solution.

findings.headline: Total arrears increased £2M to £27.8M at end of Q1, with bad debt provision rising to £25.0M, indicating deteriorating collection quality despite overall rate targets.
findings.detail: Prior-year arrears are £15.9M and in-year arrears £11.9M. The bad debt provision increased £2.4M from opening position. The council is seeking approval to write off £0.4M of historic bad debts as uneconomical to pursue, though all remain liable for collection. This reflects economic pressures on households and businesses alongside collection challenges.
findings.matters: Rising arrears and bad debt provisions indicate either weakening debtor financial position or collection effectiveness decline. Both signal economic stress in the local area and reduce forward cash flow certainty. The council's ability to recover arrears depends on underlying economic conditions improving.
findings.figures: Total arrears £27.8M (up £2M), bad debt provision £25.0M (up £2.4M), write-offs approved £0.4M
findings.quote: The table shows that the overall overdue debt (arrears) forecast at June 2026 stands at £27.8M... an increase of £2M from the opening position.

findings.headline: Treasury management underspend of £1.6M due to higher investment income and lower borrowing costs, masking underlying financial pressures.
findings.detail: The council has maintained an under-borrowed position to avoid taking on long-term borrowing at elevated PWLB rates (forecast 6.15% for 50-year Certainty rate). This strategy is yielding returns: the treasury position shows £1.6M underspend from competitive rates on short-term LA deposits and delays in capital borrowing. However, this is contingent on stable interest rates and sufficient cash reserves; it is not a structural solution to budget gaps.
findings.matters: A temporary treasury underspend is masking £3.1M of underlying service overspends. PWLB rates are expected to fall over the next 2-3 years, reducing investment returns, so this benefit will decline. The council is essentially using internal cash to defer borrowing decisions, but this consumes reserves and is not sustainable long-term.
findings.figures: £1.6M underspend: competitive short-term LA deposit rates and delays in capital borrowing
findings.quote: The capital financing budget is forecast to be £1.6M underspent by year-end. This is due to the continued benefit received from competitive rates on short-term local authority (investment) deposits together with delays in anticipated new long-term borrowing to deliver current capital priorities.

findings.headline: Agency staffing costs forecast at £4.3M, showing significant improvement from £10.6M prior year despite continued social care demand pressures.
findings.detail: The agency reduction programme is delivering results, with forecast spend down by over 60% year-on-year. However, the report notes this assumes the reduction programme continues and controls are maintained. Children's Services agency spend forecasts £1.9M (up from budget of £0.7M) due to vacancy and sickness cover needs. The improvement is fragile and dependent on successful permanent recruitment.
findings.matters: High agency costs are both a symptom of recruitment difficulties and a budget pressure. The improvement suggests the council is successfully rebuilding permanent capacity, but the continued large overspends in social care services indicate the constraint is not resolved and could reverse if permanent recruitment slows.
findings.figures: £4.3M agency spend forecast 26/27 vs £10.6M prior year. Children's Services £1.9M vs £0.7M budget.
findings.quote: This position shows a clear improvement on last year where the reported cost pressure of Agency stood in excess of £10.6M showing that the reduction programme is starting to have the desired effect.

findings.headline: Business rates collection down 1.31% against 98% target, and 1.25% below prior-year actual, reflecting economic pressures on businesses.
findings.detail: The council is forecasting 96.69% collection vs 98% target and 97.94% in 2025/26. This reflects wider economic challenges and cost pressures on businesses and comes despite additional retail, leisure and hospitality relief. Council tax collection is closer to target at 96.18% vs 96.5%, broadly in line with 2025/26. Every 0.1% change in business rates collection represents £0.1M income variance.
findings.matters: Business rates are volatile and directly exposed to economic cycles. The council's reliance on rates income has increased as government grant funding has fallen. A shortfall of 1.31% in rates income creates direct pressure on the revenue budget and is an early indicator of local economic weakness.
findings.figures: Business rates 96.69% vs 98% target (-1.31%), also 1.25% below 25/26 actual. Council tax 96.18% vs 96.5% target (-0.32%)
findings.quote: Business Rates collection is forecast to be 1.31% below the stretch target and 1.25% below the 25/26 position. This reflects wider economic challenges and increased cost pressures on businesses

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £21.2M from 2026/27 into future years, primarily CRSTS sustainable transport schemes (£20.7M) pushed to 2027/28.
findings.detail: The slippage is largely outside the council's control (A635/A633 Stairfoot Improvements and Smithies & Dearne Valley Active Travel Bridges schemes) and represents a deferral of delivery risk to the following year. Goldthorpe Housing project (£0.5M) also delayed due to revised property acquisition timing. Overall 5-year capital programme shows only £0.1M net reduction.
findings.matters: Significant year-on-year capital slippage creates refinancing risk and can indicate delivery capacity constraints or coordination problems with partner agencies (DfT in this case). It also defers economic impact and job creation outcomes.
findings.figures: £21.2M slippage from 26/27 to 27/28. CRSTS £20.7M, Goldthorpe £0.5M, other £0.1M
findings.quote: Of the total 26/27 variation in expenditure against approved plans, £21.2M relates to scheme slippage

findings.headline: Strategic reserves being drawn down in 2026/27, with any further service deterioration requiring additional unplanned deployments and reducing council financial resilience.
findings.detail: The 26/27 budget approved use of £4.2M of strategic reserves. The report explicitly states that further deterioration will require deployment of reserves "currently earmarked for other corporate priorities", which would reduce financial resilience and necessitate additional recurring savings beyond the £30M already identified. This creates a risk cycle where temporary pressures become permanent constraints.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion signals declining financial headroom and reduces the council's ability to absorb future shocks (economic downturn, emergency spending, grant changes). For lenders, depleting reserves indicates tightening liquidity and weakening balance sheet position.
findings.figures: £4.2M strategic reserve deployment planned in 26/27 budget. Current overspend of £1.5M would trigger additional unplanned deployment.
findings.quote: Note that any further deterioration in the Council's financial position during 2026/27 will require the deployment of strategic reserves currently earmarked for other corporate priorities in order to achieve a balanced budget. Such a position would reduce the Council's financial resilience and is likely to necessitate the identification and delivery of additional recurring savings over and above the £30 million required to deliver a sustainable Medium Term Financial Strategy

findings.headline: Adult Social Care forecasting £1.5M overspend due to increased provisioning costs and care demand across both Older People and Working Age Adults.
findings.detail: Older People services face £0.7M overspend from new clients and rising care costs despite reduced client contributions. Working Age Adults facing £0.8M overspend mainly from specialist residential placements and direct payment costs. The council approved an Adult Social Care Strategy for Change on 22 April 2026 targeting fee capping and service redesign, but this is in early delivery phase.
findings.matters: Adult social care is subject to the Care Act statutory duty and demand is driven by an ageing population and hospital discharge pressures. Cost increases are outpacing budget growth, and care provider fee demands continue to rise. This represents a structural pressure that will require either service specification change or sustained reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £1.5M overspend: Older People £0.7M, Working Age Adults £0.8M (including £0.9M provisioning cost pressure). £699M care cost increase for older people, £891M for working age adults.
findings.quote: Pressures within Adult Social Care have continued in 26/27 due to demands within the Working Age Specialist teams and the Older People's service. As a result, the service is currently forecasting an overspend of £1.5M at the end of the financial year.

findings.headline: Children's Social Care placement numbers increased significantly: 61 residential placements vs 50 in Q1 2025/26, and 93 IFA placements vs 76, driving £0.9M overspend.
findings.detail: The council is heavily dependent on external high-cost placements. Each additional residential placement costs over £0.4M annually on average (or £8,000 per week), and each IFA placement costs £0.057M. A new sufficiency strategy approved in April 2026 aims to address this through early intervention, in-house fostering expansion, and three new council-led residential homes, but these are delayed in implementation.
findings.matters: Placement numbers are driven by demand for statutory safeguarding duty which the council cannot refuse. Unit costs are rising faster than inflation due to market conditions and complexity of need. Without successful internal provision expansion, the overspend will worsen and consume reserves.
findings.figures: 61 residential placements (vs 50 year-ago), 93 IFA placements (vs 76), £0.9M Q1 overspend, £1.1M placement-related cost pressure
findings.quote: The Council continues to be heavily reliant on high-cost external residential placements (61 children compared with 50 as of Q1 25/26) and Independent Foster Agency (IFA) placements (93 children compared with 76 as of Q1 25/26)

findings.headline: Medium-term financial strategy gap widened to £31M-£34M through to 2029/30, up from £23M forecast in February 2026.
findings.detail: The gap increased by £8M-£11M in a single quarter. The £31M is before accounting for current Q1 service pressures of £3.1M, which would increase the gap to £34M unless mitigated. The council budgeted for £4.2M of strategic reserve depletion in 26/27 pending development of efficiency plans, but the gap trajectory suggests this will be insufficient.
findings.matters: A widening gap on this scale signals that one-year savings programmes are insufficient and structural service reductions or fundamental service redesign are likely needed. For lenders, it indicates the council will face increasing pressure on reserves and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £31M gap forecast (potentially £34M including Q1 pressures) through 2028/29-2029/30, up from £23M in February 2026. £30M recurring savings required.
findings.quote: It was estimated that the Council would face a funding gap of £23M through to the end of 28/29. To maintain a 3-year rolling position, the Council's MTFS has subsequently been rolled forward to 29/30 with the current gap now forecast to be in the region of £31M.

findings.headline: General Fund overspend of £1.5M forecast for 2026/27, with service pressures of £3.1M partly masked by £1.6M treasury underspend.
findings.detail: Service overspends total £3.1M: Children's Social Care £0.9M, Adult Social Care £1.5M, and Place Directorate £0.9M, largely driven by placement cost increases in social care. A £1.6M underspend on treasury management (lower borrowing costs and higher investment returns) is offsetting these, creating a false picture of control.
findings.matters: The treasury benefit is temporary and one-off: borrowing costs are forecast to fall over time, and investment returns depend on current market conditions. Underlying service overspends of £3.1M are structural and will require recurring mitigation or reserve depletion.
findings.figures: £3.1M service overspend, £1.6M treasury underspend, net £1.5M outturn variance
findings.quote: A projected service overspend of £3.1M is currently forecast as at the end of June. This is partly offset by a one-off underspend on Corporate budgets as a result of lower borrowing costs / additional investment income (£1.6M) giving a net outturn position of £1.5M.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forecast at £13.4M in 26/27, rising to £28M by end of 27/28, with government funding support still unannounced.
findings.detail: The DSG High Needs block overspend is driven by increasing EHCP numbers, specialist placements and 1:1 tuition demand. Government has extended the override until April 2028 but has not published detail on funding for deficits beyond 25/26. This represents the largest single financial risk in the report, with uncertainty around future support levels.
findings.matters: For councils and lenders, DSG deficits are an uncontrollable liability falling to the council after the statutory override ends. Uncertainty about government support creates material budget risk that cannot be mitigated through normal efficiency action.
findings.figures: £13.4M forecast 26/27 deficit, £28M cumulative risk by end 27/28, £17.1M overall financial risk in 26/27 after accounting for High Needs Stability grant payment from Government of £15.6M
findings.quote: An overall DSG deficit (mainly relating to SEND/High Needs funding block) of £13.4M is currently forecast in 2026/27... the deficit is expected to increase by a further £14.6M in 27/28.

findings.headline: Reducing agency staffing costs is identified as the top workforce priority, indicating current high agency reliance.
findings.detail: The workforce planning section lists 'reduce agency reliance' as the primary objective under recruitment and attraction, suggesting the council currently has elevated agency spending levels it needs to bring down as part of its broader efficiency strategy.
findings.matters: High agency staffing costs directly reduce operational efficiency and financial flexibility; councils prioritizing reduction typically indicate they view current spending in this area as unsustainably elevated.

findings.headline: Council is tolerating an electronic records management compliance risk due to cost constraints.
findings.detail: The Governance and Compliance Board has formally approved tolerating a risk around electronic records management specifically because the solutions are too expensive to implement. Paper records are being reviewed for disposal but the electronic records compliance gap remains unresolved.
findings.matters: Accepting known control weaknesses for cost reasons indicates the council is operating with known gaps and prioritizing cost control over compliance remediation, relevant to understanding the control environment and financial governance capacity.
